title: Mali Gaura

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Nat Narain, and your line was slow the lively. What did you take a second time, slowly, and what did you catch? Day one thousand one hundred four.

A postcard holds a few lines and a stamp. Nobody calls it a failed letter. Sometimes it's the thing that ends up on the fridge for years, because it said one thing and said it well. Turn the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib past Nat Narain, and you come to a section with a postcard's size and its own full heading: Mali Gaura. It's short. It's complete. And it has a guest at the end of it. Today, Mali Gaura.
screen: `A POSTCARD, NOT A FAILED LETTER.` → `A SHORT SECTION, ITS OWN HEADING.` → `MALI GAURA.`

segments.voice: Here's the first thing to notice. Mali Gaura gets the same treatment as the long ragas. The section opens with its own name at the top and an invocation of the One: Ik Onkar, Satgur Prasad, the One Creator, known by the Guru's grace. A short raga isn't treated as an appendix. In the Granth, a few pages can be a whole room. Inside, the voices are Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and then, closing the section, Bhagat Namdev, a devotee whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth alongside their own. We'll sit with Namdev's verse tomorrow. Today, the opening. Guru Ram Das begins, given here in plain English, not word for word, with a picture of seekers: adepts, searchers and silent sages, all of them turning their minds toward the Lord with longing. It's a wide view for a small room. People known for hard practices are shown with the same longing anyone can have, and the hymn's answer is that the Guru shows them the unseen Lord. That's the sweetness of a short raga. There's no time to wander. It names the longing, points to the answer, and stops. Length isn't the measure here. A short shabad sung with attention is a complete offering. Mali Gaura doesn't apologize for being brief. It simply says what it came to say, then hands the last word to a guest. That's today's line: short and sweet.
screen: `ITS OWN NAME, ITS OWN INVOCATION.` · `GURUS FIRST, NAMDEV LAST.` · `SEEKERS AND SAGES, ALL LONGING.` · `LENGTH ISN'T THE MEASURE.` · then, large: `SHORT AND SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one short thing, held whole. Sit and settle. Choose one short word to stay with: if you pray, Waheguru; if you don't, simply the word here. Say it once, silently, and let it be complete. Don't stack more words behind it. When the mind starts writing a longer letter, set the pen down and come back to the postcard: one word, one breath. Each time is enough on its own. Later today, find one shabad from Mali Gaura and listen to it once, start to finish. The bell holds the time.
Mali Gaura. A short raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, with its own heading and invocation, where Gurus sing first and Bhagat Namdev closes. Today's word.
Your line: short and sweet. Once today, say something important in fewer words than you'd usually use, and then stop talking. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Each raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in its own raga in kirtan; shorter sections like Mali Gaura are drawn on just as the longer ones are, and a single shabad is a complete offering in a gurdwara program.
